messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory
  - Threat

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Memory → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory → Threat
  - Threat → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat → Memory
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Memory
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Threat

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Kwame is a 62-year-old stock broker, divorced for nearly a decade, who lost his 35-year-old son in a hit-and-run nine months ago. The call came mid-morning on the trading floor; he drove straight to the county morgue but can only recall the fluorescent lights and the sheet pulled back—his son’s hand, still warm, then gone. What stays with him are fragments that arrive without warning: the ringing phone, the smell of antiseptic, a stranger’s voice saying “fatal.” He cannot deliberately retrieve the whole sequence—it feels locked behind a door he cannot open. These sudden pieces force him to go over and over why this happened to him, why the driver never stopped, why he wasn’t there to prevent it. He spends hours on the sofa turning the same questions, hoping to pin down an answer that never comes. At the same time, he tries hard not to think about the accident at all—switching channels, leaving the room when grief comes up—but the fragments keep breaking through. Because he cannot access the full memory, his mind keeps circling back, trying to fill the gaps with rumination and suppression.

The fragments also unleash overwhelming guilt and anger—strong negative feelings that flare whenever an image surfaces. Sometimes he feels the accident is happening again: the same roar in his ears, the same helplessness, as if he is back in the morgue. Those flashbacks frighten him most because they blur the line between past and present. In response to that threat, he doubles down on avoiding everything that might trigger it—his son’s photo, the street where it happened, even conversations about cars. Yet the avoidance does not settle his fear; instead the intrusions become more frequent, and his deliberate recall grows even harder. He now finds he can barely describe the drive to the hospital, as if the act of pushing away has erased pieces he might have held.

His rumination—repeatedly asking why this happened to him—deepens the guilt and self-blame, making him feel he deserves something terrible in return. That belief has started to show in his trading: he takes wildly excessive risks on speculative stocks, sometimes betting the whole account on a single rumor. He knows it is dangerous, but part of him welcomes the danger, as if the market’s punishment might match what he feels inside. These reckless moves, in turn, send his adrenaline surging, and when the market swings he finds himself back in the morgue, flooded by a fragment he cannot name. The cycle tightens: the more he rues, the more guilt he feels; the more guilt, the more he risks; the more risk, the more the memories intrude.

By now Kwame’s social world has shrunk. He stopped meeting friends for dinner because someone might mention his son. He quit the grief group after one session—the shared stories felt too close to his own. At work his desk is piled with trades that alarm his manager, but he brushes off the warnings. What finally brought him to therapy was a panic attack two weeks ago on the subway, triggered by a stranger’s sneeze that sounded like the phone ringing that morning. He is terrified that he is losing control—not just of his memory, but of the reckless part of himself that seems to want to crash. He hopes that by making sense of the fragments he can stop the spiral before it costs him everything. That persistent sense of danger kept the accident hovering just inside his awareness, ready to surface unexpectedly.
